text: Of course, both tools are under active development, so I don't know how long these observations will hold true. It will be interesting to see whether they start to converge, or whether their current differences result in increasingly different use cases.

author: RosieCampbell
text: Obsidian is where notes become legible to others and ready to publish. It's also the system I use to preserve ideas for future Rosie, secure in the knowledge that they are in a standardized format.

author: RosieCampbell
text: Obsidian is best for longer-form, more fully-formed, 'permanent' notes. It's where notes become essays and articles. They take on clarity and structure via markdown, and it's motivating to seem them beautifully rendered.

author: RosieCampbell
text: Roam is where I instinctively go to capture things quickly and search for them later, knowing I can use queries and filters to pinpoint precisely what I need. It's messy and high-context. Roam is my day-to-day private thinking companion.

author: RosieCampbell
text: Roam is best for creative idea generation, quick random thoughts, effortless entry, playful exploration, and making connections.

author: RosieCampbell
text:
(Side note: Backlinks are fantastic, but if you think they are the majority of the value of either of these applications, you're missing out)

So where does that leave things? In my opinion:

author: RosieCampbell
text: Because Obsidian is aiming to be as future-proof and standardized as possible, notes are pure markdown (no custom metadata). This limits the range of possible features, but is as close as you can get to knowing you'll be able to read your notes in 50 years time.

author: RosieCampbell
text: Obsidian on the other hand is based on locally-stored markdown files. You have complete control; you can open them in any markdown editor without needing to export, so you do things like use VS Code to do a regex find&replace across all notes. Not (currently) possible in Roam

author: RosieCampbell
text: As with many things, this strength (custom metadata for fancy features) is also a weakness. You can export to markdown, but if you've made a lot of use of proprietary Roam features, the resulting files may not be that useful (or at least, they'll be messy and somewhat illegible)

author: RosieCampbell
text: Roam is fundamentally a database. Blocks are atomic, and uniquely identifiable. This affords it outliner functionality and block-level manipulation. Behind the scenes, database metadata enables fancy features like block references, kanban boards, diagrams, etc.

text: @TonyChurnside I wonder if they realize it's not how UK schools actually are

author: RosieCampbell
text: I assume it's an attempt to appeal to both sides of the Atlantic? I quite like it but it's kind of surreal. I guess the word I'm looking for is anatopistic

author: RosieCampbell
text: Noticing a trend on Netflix of TV shows set in the UK but with American aesthetics (e.g. no school uniform, letterman jackets, 50s style diners, etc). Examples include Sex Education and The End of the F***ing World

author: RosieCampbell
text: What I suspect in reality is that different approaches work for different people, but that most of our attention has gone towards rules-based approaches (perhaps because they are more straightforward) and we could benefit from more innovative ideas for intuitive approaches

author: RosieCampbell
text: If intuitive eating is real and works, I wonder if similar principles can also help us work *with* our internal motivation for more sustainable and pleasant work practices, rather than constantly trying to override it in the pursuit of short-term productivity

author: RosieCampbell
text: Perhaps binging Netflix when you know you should be working is the equivalent of binging food to rebel against an oppressive eating regime

author: RosieCampbell
text: My intuition is that in both cases these strict approaches can be useful tools, but that perhaps they can interfere with our ability to listen to what our bodies need, to potentially detrimental effect

author: RosieCampbell
text: A lot of this feels like it has parallels in diet culture (restricting certain foods, eating only at certain times, counting calories/macros etc)

author: RosieCampbell
text: Whereas I feel like a lot of productivity advice involves strict rules that aim to override our inclinations, e.g. blocking distracting apps, following habit checklists, pomodoros that instruct you when to work and when to rest regardless of how you're feeling, etc

author: RosieCampbell
text: We kind of do this with sleep already - pretty much everyone now accepts that we all need different amounts of sleep, and that it's better to listen to your natural body clock than force yourself to be a morning person if you're not

author: RosieCampbell
text: I'm reading a book on intuitive eating (i.e. rejecting restrictive eating rules in favor of listening carefully to your body's satiety cues) and am wondering where else it might be wise to apply this concept
